Direct answer | Genetic counselors on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 29-9092.00. Work falls into several categories: (one) Family history and risk assessment: interview patients or review records to obtain and document complete patient or family histories and analyze genetic information to identify disease or syndrome risks. (two) Pretest counseling and informed decisions: discuss testing options, risks, benefits, and limitations and explain questions testing can and cannot answer. (three) Post-test interpretation and disclosure: interpret laboratory results, communicate to patients or physicians, and explain positive, negative, and uncertain results and implications for relatives. (four) Specialty counseling: counsel in prenatal, pediatric, cancer, neurologic, and other clinical genetics areas and explain inheritance of cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer's disease, diabetes, and cancers. (five) Psychosocial support and referral: assess stress, fear of results, financial issues, marital conflicts, and other psychological or emotional needs and recommend referral or support coping. (six) Reports, follow-up, and research: write detailed reports explaining complex genetics to patients or referring physicians, read literature and attend professional meetings, and possibly assist genetic research. The cycle connects referral and scheduling—family and medical history—risk assessment and testing discussion—test request and interpretation—disclosure and psychological support—reports, referral, and follow-up. This page distinguishes this occupation from clinical and counseling psychologists, clinical neuropsychologists, physician assistants, clinical nurse specialists, geneticists, and medical and health services managers. Counseling duties do not extend to independent clinical diagnosis, treatment, or statutory medical assessment.

O*NET and BLS occupational-profile highlights | This page covers U.S. SOC 29-9092.00, Genetic Counselors, a healthcare occupation updated by O*NET in 2026 and labeled Bright Outlook. The official scope is individual or family risk assessment for inherited conditions such as genetic disorders and birth defects; information for providers or concerned individuals and families; advice supporting informed decisions and coping; and possible assistance with genetic-condition or counseling research. Core O*NET tasks include counseling patients and families with information, education, or reassurance, importance 100; analyzing genetic information to identify patients or families at risk for particular diseases or syndromes, 99; counseling in prenatal, pediatric, cancer, neurologic, and other clinical genetics specialties, 99; discussing testing options, risks, benefits, and limitations for informed decisions, 99; interviewing patients or reviewing records for complete documented patient or family histories, 98; explaining inheritance of cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer's disease, diabetes, and cancers, 97; interpreting laboratory results and communicating them to patients or physicians, 97; writing detailed consultation reports explaining complex genetics, 93; following advances through literature and professional organizations and meetings, 93; and assessing psychological or emotional needs and recommending referral or helping patients cope with results, 93. What personality is better suited to genetic counseling? This occupation places greater weight on rigorous evidence and risk judgment, the ability to explain complex concepts clearly, empathy and stability when facing bad news and uncertain results, and willingness to protect patient and family confidentiality, rather than any personality type. O*NET lists the interest code ISC (Investigative—Social—Conventional), and work styles emphasizing sincerity, empathy, stress tolerance, self-control, cooperation, intellectual curiosity, caution, integrity, and attention to detail. These can be starting points for exploration.

Can introverts do this work? Yes, but communication is very frequent (email daily 100%, face-to-face or individual and team discussions daily 95%, telephone daily 90%, constant contact with others 67%). Clear, gentle communication is also required when delivering bad news or addressing family conflict.
Can extroverts do well? Extroversion does not establish communication effectiveness. Observe whether risks are explained, feedback is heard, and checks and records are completed.

Which MBTI type is best for this occupation? No type has been shown to be best. MBTI is not an assessment of professional qualifications or abilities. Career adjustment mainly depends on genetics knowledge, communication, ethics, and stress tolerance.

Which Holland interest types are more relevant to this occupation? O*NET lists ISC: Investigative (researching and analyzing disease, genetics, and data), Social (helping and educating others), and Conventional (organizing information and records according to standards). Use this to explore task preferences, not to predict performance.

Can personality predict performance? This page has not established predictive validity for this occupation, so scores cannot support individual fit conclusions. Check fictional tasks and real qualification assessments separately.

Can someone who struggles with math do this work? Observe whether they can check probabilities, ratios, and units under stated assumptions and explain uncertainty. This page has not established a universal mathematics threshold and does not claim that advanced mathematics is unnecessary. G1 checks only the arithmetic in this exercise; professional training requires separate verification.

Does this occupation require high emotional intelligence? It requires empathy, emotional stability, stress management, and conflict resolution skills, but no specific assessment score. The work involves sustained exposure to uncertain results, bad news, and family emotions, requiring personal and team support.

Can the Enneagram determine whether I am suited to this work? No. The Enneagram is a self-exploration tool, not a conclusion about occupational ability or fit. Evaluate whether you can accurately collect family histories, assess risks, communicate findings, keep records, and escalate within your scope of practice and ethical requirements.

Use the complete G1 materials. The three tables and draft show checking performance in this exercise. Record errors and unknowns against the answers; a single short task cannot establish long-term fit, hiring suitability, or clinical ability.

values: M1, a fictional three-generation pedigree: I01 and I02 are the parents of II01; I03 and I04 are the parents of II02; II01 and II02 are the parents of III01. All seven people are identified only by ID and relationship; ages and phenotypes are not provided. Missing information must not be treated as evidence of disease or absence of disease.

M2, the stipulated arithmetic model: Assume II01 is Aa and II02 is aa. II01 transmits A or a with probability 0.5 each; II02 transmits only a. The exercise stipulates that an A carrier has probability 0.60 of expressing a fictional trait. This has no correspondence to real diseases, test results, or the health of people in M1.

M3, fictional test report B01: specimen S01, subject III01, result VUS. No diagnostic basis or evidence connecting it to model M2 is provided, yet the draft says, 'Confirmed diagnosis, model probability 3%.' A VUS must not be used to confirm or exclude disease.

M4, fictional consent form C01: III01 health information is solely for a controlled internal counseling exercise; public groups and external AI services are not authorized. Request R1, received at 09:00, asks for the complete pedigree and B01 to be sent to a public group before 09:30.

M5, fictional follow-up form F01: registered date 2026-10-05, draft date 2026-10-15. It was handed to coordinator Q for verification at 09:10, with no response by 09:12. Do not mark it confirmed or completed.

M6: Draw three tables yourself. The pedigree/source table lists IDs, relationships, sources, and missing items. The checking table lists material IDs, original values, draft values, calculations/questions, and handling status. The counseling and handover draft lists testing limitations, model assumptions, privacy boundaries, recipient roles, pending confirmations, and acknowledgments. Only paper, a pen, and a calculator are needed; no external template is required.

A 60-minute paper exercise, G1: Use M1—M6 to complete three tables and a pretest counseling draft. Spend the first 15 minutes checking identities, relationships, and missing information, the next 15 minutes on calculations and discrepancy checks, another 20 minutes on privacy and follow-up handover, and the final 10 minutes checking your work against the answers.

Calculate the model probabilities of carrying A and expressing the trait, compare them with the draft's 3%, and explain ratios/percentage points. Check the difference between follow-up dates and the time remaining from 09:12 to the public-group request deadline.

Record at least the two risks of treating a VUS as a confirmed diagnosis and unauthorized public disclosure. Pause unverified conclusions and public transmission while retaining lawful information checks and explanations of limitations. Record pending confirmation from laboratory/authorized clinical personnel and the coordinator's acknowledgment.

Reference check: II01 and II02 have different pairs of parents, and the parents of III01 are specified. Ages and phenotypes are absent; record them as unknown rather than inventing them. In M2, offspring have probability 0.5 each of Aa or aa, giving a 50% probability of carrying A. The stipulated expression probability is 0.5×0.60=0.30, or 30%. This is only an arithmetic model and cannot provide the real risk for III01.

The draft's 3% is 0.03; the correct model's 30% is 0.30. The difference is 27 percentage points, and the draft is 1/10 of the correct model value. There is no evidence connecting the VUS in B01 to M2. Do not reclassify it as confirming or excluding a diagnosis, or treat the model explanation as clinical advice.

The two dates in F01 differ by 10 days; list this conflict as pending confirmation by Q. From the 09:10 handover to 09:12, 2 minutes have passed without acknowledgment; from 09:12 to 09:30, 18 minutes remain. Do not claim follow-up is confirmed or transmission is complete.

Keep public disclosure under R1 paused. Explain that C01 does not authorize that purpose, and refer the matter to the information permissions owner to check the lawful basis and recipient scope. If no reply has arrived, keep the status as not acknowledged.

entries.answer: Genetic counselors on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 29-9092.00: they assess individual or family risk for various inherited conditions, such as genetic disorders and birth defects; provide information to other healthcare providers or individuals and families concerned about inherited-condition risks; counsel individuals and families to support informed decisions and coping; and may assist research related to genetic conditions or genetic counseling. Core work includes interviewing patients or reviewing medical records to obtain and document a complete family medical history; analyzing genetic information to identify patients or families at risk for particular diseases or syndromes; providing genetic counseling in specific clinical genetics fields such as prenatal care, pediatrics, oncology, and neurology; discussing testing options and their risks, benefits, and limitations with patients and families to support informed decisions; interpreting laboratory results and communicating them to patients or physicians; assessing psychological or emotional needs and recommending referrals; writing detailed consultation reports; and keeping up with genetics advances. Common employers include healthcare and social assistance organizations and other industries including educational services. This page uses U.S. occupational classification coverage.

entries.answer: The main differences concern the focus of work and level of authorization. This occupation focuses on counseling, information interpretation, and psychological support related to genetic risks and testing, producing verifiable consultation reports and records. Clinical and counseling psychologists (19-3033.00) focus on psychological assessment, diagnosis, and psychotherapy; clinical neuropsychologists on neuropsychological testing and cognitive function assessment; physician assistants (29-1071.00) undertake some diagnosis and treatment within supervised or collaborative practice; clinical nurse specialists (29-1141.04) focus on specialist nursing and care coordination; geneticists (19-1029.03) on basic and applied genetics research; and medical and health services managers (11-9111.00) on healthcare institution operations and management. Their focus and authorization levels differ. Permissions for diagnosis, treatment, procedures, laboratory testing, and statutory appraisal cannot be carried over between roles.

entries.answer: Common failures include incomplete family history, incorrect pedigree interpretation, or treating uncertain results or results of uncertain significance as confirming or excluding a diagnosis; clinical diagnosis, testing, or procedures beyond the scope of practice or institutional authorization, or failure to obtain informed consent; inadequate explanation of testing limitations and family implications, inappropriate delivery of bad news, or lack of psychological support and referral; false, missing, or retrospectively modified consultation reports, testing, informed consent, and follow-up records; leaks, unauthorized access, or unauthorized external provision of sensitive genetic, pedigree, and testing information; and key counseling work dependent on one person or unclear referral and follow-up handovers. subject.name: Genetic Counselors
subject.summary: Genetic counselors correspond to U.S. O*NET / SOC 29-9092.00, Genetic Counselors: assess individual or family risk for inherited conditions such as genetic disorders and birth defects; provide information to healthcare providers or individuals and families concerned about such risks; advise individuals and families to support informed decisions and coping; and may assist research related to genetic conditions or counseling. Core work includes interviewing patients or reviewing medical records to obtain and document complete patient or family histories; analyzing genetic information to identify patients or families at risk for particular diseases or syndromes; counseling in prenatal, pediatric, cancer, neurologic, or other clinical genetics specialties; discussing testing options, risks, benefits, and limitations to support informed decisions; interpreting laboratory results and communicating them to patients or physicians; assessing psychological or emotional needs and recommending referrals; writing detailed consultation reports; and keeping up with genetic advances. Official scope: Assess individual or family risk for a variety of inherited conditions, such as genetic disorders and birth defects. Provide information to other healthcare providers or to individuals and families concerned with the risk of inherited conditions. Advise individuals and families to support informed decisionmaking and coping methods for those at risk. May help conduct research related to genetic conditions or genetic counseling.
